questions.question: What motivated you to go on exchange? (pick the most important one) *
questions.answer: Explore new cultures

questions.question: Which aspects were crucial to choosing your study destination? *
questions.answer: Location, culture

questions.question: How would you rate your overall study abroad experience? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: Great experience! I enjoyed every day in Switzerland and felt very much at home.

questions.question: How easy was it to find the information you needed to know upon arrival? *
questions.answer: I was a bit unsure about a couple of things since I did not receive anything on mail but only on Mobility Online, and I was not aware of that in the start of the proces. As soon as I realized, it was super easy to gather all important information in order to be prepared for my stay. The communication with the Swiss University was great and they provided me with all the information I needed.

questions.question: What assistance, if any, did you receive when you arrived at your study destination? *
questions.answer: I did not receive any from the university, but I had a feeling that I could contact the International Office to get support in case I would need it at some point. I lived with a lot of other exchange students in a student housing which meant that we supported each other and shared information about the different processes of moving to another country, getting to know the university and so on.

questions.question: Overall, how satisfied were you with the orientation and assistance available to students at your host institution upon arrival? *
Additional comments
questions.answer: I am not fully aware of the different options available and therefore I do not think that I am the right one to answer this question. Overall I am happy with the orientation even though I would have liked to have understood the structures at the university a bit earlier. However, I think it might have been my own responsibility and therefore mistake.

questions.question: How did you find housing? *
questions.answer: I found housing through my host institution

questions.question: Did you live on campus or off campus? *
questions.answer: Off campus

questions.question: How easy was it to find off campus housing? Any recommendations? *
questions.answer: It was very easy! The Swiss university sent out information about applying for student housing, deadliens and so on. From then on everything was communicated directly from the student housing office, which were also very helpful and informative. At first, I did not receive the e-mail with a housing offer, so I had to contact them in order to have it re-sent. I got it the same day and since then everything worked smoothly. Zürich is super expensive and living there even more so, so I can only recommend contacting the local student housing offices (there is a couple of different options) when searching for accommodation. The only "problem" is that rental contracts are usually fixed and cannot be shortened/prolonged freely - depends from house to house though. In my house we were allowed to rent our room out for a maximum of two months, which was very nice for the people who left right after the exams. Be aware that the semester start/end is different and that the spring semester is usually one month longer than the fall semester.

questions.question: What should future exchange students know about living off campus? *
questions.answer: It was great. There is not a lot of options to live on campus and the ones there is is usually for local students. It is possible to stay in student housing associations on campus, but these requires way more work, applying long in advance, detailed applications, interviews and more. For that reason, I think the student housing options around town are the easiest and most convenient way for exchange students to find a place to stay. This also makes exploration of the city more natural and you get to see a lot of new areas without putting in any effort - simply because traveling through town is a way of exploring.

questions.question: Overall, how satisfied were you with the housing available to students? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: Very! However, the house I stayed in was not the most comfortable. The rooms and common facilities were great except that we were 170 exchange students sharing ONE(!) kitchen. This was not always clean, convenient or nice to use, and for that reason I might have preferred a smaller housing option. However, it allowed me to meet tons of new people at home and therefore I felt at home very easily.

questions.question: How easy did you find the registration process at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: Super easy. Everything happened through mobility online and it worked very well.

questions.question: Please describe the registration process at your host institution *
questions.answer: I uploaded the documents needed and afterwards received a letter of admission. Afterwards I received a lot of different information about registration in home commune and immigration office, health insurance and so on.

questions.question: What kind of help was available? *
questions.answer: I could e-mail the office of international affairs at any time if needed. I did however no use their offers.

questions.question: How successful were you in registering for the classes you wanted? *
questions.answer: Very. It was super easy to do online. However, non-german speakers might face a challenge when registering since a larger part of the information is only available in German.

questions.question: What advice would you offer to future exchange students about registration at your host institution? *
questions.answer: At UZH you can change your courses within the first two weeks of the semester. This allows you to try out all the courses you find interesting and then pick the ones you like the most in the end. You can for example sign up for 45 ECTS, attend them all for the first week and then pick the ones you like the most/change them all completely. I was not 100% sure about how this worked at first and would have liked a bit more information about this, but it worked out well and I was very happy for this system. Note that in some faculties the courses are rather small (2-6 ECTS) and therefore you'd have to pick a lot of different courses to reach the right number of credits. This requires you to check all class times AND locations carefully, since courses can overlap and/or be held in completely different campuses in the city making it impossible to get to class in time/attend the whole class. Some courses are live online, some are recorded and some required physical attendance - check it out before signing up.

questions.question: How satisfied were you with the academic programme at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: It was great. Good options for English-speaking exchange students.

questions.question: Were you a BA or MA student at UCPH when you were on exchange? *
questions.answer: BA

questions.question: Please elaborate on the level of courses *
questions.answer: I studied with both BA and MA students. The level was fine all over and I am very satisfied. However, spending the first 1-2 weeks of the semester finding out which courses suit you best is a good idea. I for example found that some courses required way more preparation than others even though the number of credits was the same. Some are passed through a multiple choice test and others require you to write a 5 page essay to the texts of the week every week the whole semester. In one case I changed subject because the level was too high and the field was new to me.

questions.question: How did the style of teaching at your host institution compare with that of UCPH? *
questions.answer: I experienced several teaching styles, but the biggest difference was that I did not have any group work in my courses. This was nice, because it gave me flexibility to explore the country, but it also made it very hard to meet local students from the host country. I expected the instructors to be more authoritarian, but they were all very kind, open and inclusive.

questions.question: How long were you on exchange? *
questions.answer: 1 semester

questions.question: Please list the courses you were enrolled in during your first semester. *
questions.answer:
- Animal Ethics
- Media Management
- Communication, Technology and Urban Life
- Digital Well-Being
- Global Switzerland: From Early Globalizer to International Geneva
- Summer School: What defines a country's succes? 
- German Courses (B1 Diskutieren + B2 Lesen & Schreiben)

questions.question: What specific courses would you recommend to future exchange students? Why? *
questions.answer:
Animal ethics was great and a very special course for people from many different fields. Here we discussed literature and philosophy on animal ethics. The learning environment was very comfortable and we all learned from each other when discussing different aspects of animal rights.

Digital Well-being taught me a lot about the significance of creating healthy frames around the use of digitized solutions, products and platforms. Since this is expected to increase in importance in the future, it is very interesting to learn about. Unfortunately, it was a bit far from my study since it also includes big data and the like, which I have never worked with as a language and communication science student. 

I can also recommend Global Switzerland and the summer school. These courses are made for exchange students and students from many different fields can participate. It is multidisciplinary and they also work as an academic introduction to the country you'll live in (historically, socially, economically, politically).

What unexpected costs did you encounter? *
questions.answer: It is obligatory to have a private health insurance. They pay almost all expenses to doctors and so on. However, if you do not work in Switzerland and you are covered by the common European health insurance, you can get an exemption from the insurance. This is nice, but it means that you have to pay all doctor bills at first and then send it to the organization afterwards. I think it is a good option to get a private health insurance which covers everything, because EU do not pay everything, but it is expensive and therefore it might make more sense for some to get an insurance through a Danish company while still getting the exemption from a Swiss insurance. Also, several companies offer cheap additional health insurances, but these are usually not good and it has proven to be very hard to get money back from them. Therefore it is important to fix these things in time.

questions.question: What items were more or less expensive than you expected? *
questions.answer: Food is incredibly expensive. I spent approximately 40% more on food than I do when I am in Denmark. Also, public transportation is expensive especially if you are over 25 years old. SBB has good offers making it more affordable to travel by train, but normal tickets for people who do not use these offers (Snow25, half fare and more) are super super expensive if you travel out of the city of Zürich.

questions.question: How satisfied were you with the non-academic opportunities (clubs, sports, etc.) at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
What kinds of cultural, athletic and social activities were available for students at your host institution? *
questions.answer:
Zürich and the surrounding unis has the best student sports association! All sports from pilates to hiking, biking, football, strengt training, climbing, ski touring and to sailing and surfing are included (100+!). Most are free and there is hundreds of activities to sign up for every day. There is also great facilities such as sport halls, gym, sauna and more. This is the greatest and I can only recommend!
Weekly bars and coffee clubs at uni were harder to get to know since they are located in many different areas. If you do not know local students well, you probably wont go. The big shared bar BKVM is however a great place for everyone to meet.
Erasmus also arranges tons of activities, which is also a great way to meet new people and explore new places.

questions.question: Which non -academic activities would you recommend to future exchange students? Why? *
questions.answer: All ASVZ activities!

questions.question: What do you recommend other visiting students see or do on their weekends or holidays? *
questions.answer: Go to the mountains! Skiing in winter and hiking in summer. The nature is amazing! SBB and the local ski resorts have a lot of different offers (such as Snow25) for students and young people, so you can go skiing at a reasonable price. Also, the Half Fare train card gives you half price of all travels in Switzerland for 1 year - if you intend on exploring the country, this is usually worth it!

questions.question: How easy was it to adjust to the local culture of your exchange site? *
questions.answer: Very easy! City reminded me a bit of home and I felt at home very fast.

questions.question: Do you have any tips for socializing with local students?
questions.answer: Go to ASVZ sport activities.

questions.question: What, if any, cultural differences did you find particularly challenging? *
questions.answer: Everything is closed on Sundays. Besides of that, no challenges.

questions.question: What parts of the culture did you most appreciate? *
questions.answer: Everything is very clean, well-maintained and punctual. Also, the Swiss really appreciate the nature which means that they 1) clean up after themselves 2) love going on trips and adventures and 3) they adapt to the weather and have fun activities to do all year. The people respect each other and each other's privacy, but if you initiates contact, they are very friendly and helpful!

questions.question: What are the three most important things you would tell a UCPH student who is going to your host institution on exchange? *
questions.answer: Buy yourself some good hiking boots. Bring more money than you think you'll need. Do not forget swimsuit and a rain jacket - they are equally important!

questions.question: Is there any other information that you think might prove useful to future exchange students attending your host institution? *
questions.answer: Information about insurance and in particular private health insurance is important. Also, do not forget to apply for scholarships beforehand - the country is so expensive for foreigners that extra finances can be ver helpful.

questions.question: What was the most rewarding part of your exchange experience? *
questions.answer: Exploring the culture and in particular the nature.

questions.question: What was the greatest challenge during the exchange? *
questions.answer: Learning and writing in academic English took a bit of getting-used-to.

questions.question: Any other comments?
questions.answer: Go to Switzerland!

questions.question: Do you agree to share your travel report with other fellow students? *
questions.answer: Yes
